t.5.24.1: Speaking thus, her face streaming with tears, the young Janakātmajā, her face turned downward, began to lament.
t.5.24.2: Like one mad, like one distracted, like one whose mind is bewildered, she grieved, rolling over and writhing on the surface of the earth like a young filly.
t.5.24.3: Seized and overpowered, I was carried away by force, screaming, from the vigilant Rāghava by Rāvaṇa, the rākṣasa who takes any form at will.
t.5.24.4: Fallen into the power of the rākṣasīs, being threatened most cruelly, brooding and afflicted with deep sorrow, I cannot bear to live.
t.5.24.5: For I, dwelling amid the rākṣasīs without Rāma, the great chariot-warrior, have no use for life, nor for wealth, nor for ornaments.
t.5.24.6: Shame on me, ignoble and unfaithful woman that I am, who, separated from him and living a sinful life, preserve my life even for a moment!
t.5.24.7: What desire have I for life or for happiness without him, my beloved, the sweet-spoken lord of the earth that is bounded by the ocean?
t.5.24.8: Let it be cut to pieces or even devoured; I give up this body. Separated from my beloved, I cannot endure this sorrow for long.
t.5.24.9: I would not touch that night-roamer Rāvaṇa even with my left foot; how much less would I desire him, that despicable one!
t.5.24.11: Whether I am cut, split, or hacked to pieces, or burned in a blazing fire, I would not go to Rāvaṇa. What use is your long prattle?
t.5.24.10: He who, fixed in his cruel nature, seeks to woo me does not know that he has been rejected; he knows neither himself nor his own lineage.
t.5.24.12: Rāghava is renowned as wise, grateful, compassionate and of virtuous conduct; yet I suspect he has become pitiless because my good fortune has run out.
t.5.24.13: He who single-handedly struck down fourteen thousand rākṣasas in Janasthāna, why does he not come to me?
t.5.24.14: I am held captive by Rāvaṇa, a rākṣasa of little valour; surely my husband is able to slay Rāvaṇa in battle.
t.5.24.15: Rāma, by whom Virādha, the foremost of the Rākṣasas, was slain in battle in the Daṇḍaka forest, why does he not come to me?
t.5.24.16: Granted, this Laṅkā, set in the middle of the ocean, is hard to assail; but nothing exists that can obstruct the course of Rāghava's arrows.
t.5.24.17: What, then, is the reason why Rāma, of steadfast valour, does not come to rescue his beloved wife, carried off by a rākṣasa?
t.5.24.18: I suspect that the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa does not know that I am here; for if he knew, would that mighty one endure such an outrage?
t.5.24.19: Even the king of vultures, who, having learned of me, might have reported to Rāghava that I had been carried off, was struck down in battle by Rāvaṇa.
t.5.24.20: A great deed was done by Jaṭāyus, who, though old, came to my rescue then and stood firm in single combat with Rāvaṇa.
t.5.24.21: If that Rāghava knew that I am living here, then today, enraged, he would with his arrows make the world empty of rākṣasas.
t.5.24.22: He would shatter the city of Laṅkā and dry up the great ocean, and he would destroy both the fame and the very name of the vile Rāvaṇa.
t.5.24.23: Then, there is no doubt, Rāma together with Lakṣmaṇa, having searched out the Laṅkā of the rākṣasas, would bring it about that in house after house the rākṣasīs, their lords slain, weep again just as I am weeping now.
t.5.24.24: For no enemy seen by those two lives even for a moment. Before long this Laṅkā will become like a cremation ground, a pyre whose roads are choked with smoke and which is thronged with circling flocks of vultures.
t.5.24.25: In a very short time I shall surely attain my heart's desire; this ill-fated course proclaims the ruin of all of you.
t.5.24.26: Such are the inauspicious omens now seen in Laṅkā that, in a very short time indeed, she will be stripped of her splendor.
t.5.24.27: Surely, when the wicked Rāvaṇa, lord of the Rākṣasas, is slain, Laṅkā, now hard to assail, will wither away like a young woman made a widow.
t.5.24.29: Surely, before long, I shall hear here in house after house the cries of the Rākṣasa maidens, weeping and stricken with grief.
t.5.24.28: The city of Laṅkā, now rich with the festivities of Puṣya, will, together with its rākṣasas, be bereft of its lord, like a woman whose husband has perished.
t.5.24.30: Burnt by the arrows of Rāma, the city of Laṅkā will be plunged into darkness, its radiance destroyed and its foremost Rākṣasas slain.
t.5.24.31: If only that hero Rāma, with the corners of his eyes reddened, were to know that I am living in the abode of Rāvaṇa!
t.5.24.32: The time limit that was set for me by this cruel and vile Rāvaṇa, its hour has now arrived.
t.5.24.33: The Nairṛtas, doers of evil, who do not know what ought not to be done, will now surely meet a great calamity arising from their unrighteousness.
t.5.24.34: These flesh-eating rākṣasas do not know dharma. Surely the rākṣasa will make me into his breakfast.
t.5.24.35: How shall I, deeply grieving, manage without him, Rāma, pleasing to behold, whose eyes are red at the corners, unable as I am to see him?
t.5.24.36: If only there were someone here today to give me poison, then, without my husband, I would quickly behold the god Vaivasvata.
t.5.24.38: Surely, from grief for me alone, that hero, the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa, has abandoned his body upon the earth and gone from here to the world of the gods.
t.5.24.37: Rāma, the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa, did not know that I was alive; for if the two of them knew it, they would surely not fail to search for me across the earth.
t.5.24.39: Blessed are the gods together with the Gandharvas, and the Siddhas and the supreme seers, who behold my lord Rāma, the lotus-eyed one.
t.5.24.40: Or rather, it is not indeed for his sake that I, the wife of Rāma, that wise royal sage of supreme soul who is devoted to dharma, should…
t.5.24.41: While one is in sight, a person may be well-disposed; for one who no longer sees, there is no friendship. The ungrateful destroy it, but Rāma will not destroy it.
t.5.24.42: Have I then no virtues at all, or is it indeed that my good fortune is exhausted, that I, Sītā, a lovely woman, am bereft of Rāma, who is worthy of the very best?
t.5.24.43: For me, who am separated from the great-souled Rāma, the hero of unblemished conduct and slayer of his foes, it is better to die than to live.
t.5.24.44: Or else those two brothers, the best of men, having laid aside their weapons, are wandering in the forest, living on roots and fruits, as dwellers of the woods.
t.5.24.45: Or perhaps the two heroic brothers, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, have been slain through treachery by the evil-souled Rāvaṇa, lord of the Rākṣasas.
t.5.24.46: Now that things have come to such a pass, I wish to die by any means; yet death has not been ordained for me, even though I dwell in this sorrow.
t.5.24.47: Blessed indeed are the great-souled sages, esteemed for their truthfulness, self-controlled and highly fortunate, for whom there exists neither the pleasant nor the unpleasant.
t.5.24.49: Abandoned here by my beloved Rāma, whose self is known, and fallen into the power of the wicked Rāvaṇa, I shall give up my life.
t.5.24.48: Would sorrow not arise from what is dear? And from what is not dear comes even greater fear. Salutations to those great-souled ones who are set free from both.
